analysis.one_liner: Suspends most US arms sales to Saudi Arabia and sanctions those blocking Yemen aid or killing Jamal Khashoggi.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill was referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on November 15, 2018 and never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would suspend most US weapons sales to Saudi Arabia — bombs, ammunition, vehicles, and aircraft — through September 2020, and cut off US in-flight refueling of Saudi coalition planes bombing Yemen. It would impose financial sanctions and visa bans on people blocking humanitarian aid from reaching Yemeni civilians, and on anyone responsible for murdering the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, including Saudi royal family members. It was introduced by a Democrat with three Republican cosponsors but never got so much as a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Yemeni civilians, who would face less bombardment with US-supplied weapons and US-fueled planes, and get relief supplies delivered more freely; US taxpayers, who would stop paying to refuel coalition aircraft; and journalists and dissidents, who would see US sanctions finally applied to the people behind Khashoggi's murder.

how_it_helps.text: Bars US sales or export licenses to Saudi Arabia for weapons in Munitions List categories III, IV, VII, and VIII (ammunition, ground vehicles, aircraft, and bombs) until September 30, 2020, with an exception only for ground-based missile defense.
Prohibits any US funds from being used for in-flight refueling of Saudi or Saudi-led coalition aircraft flying combat missions in the Yemen civil war.
Requires the President to impose asset-blocking sanctions and visa bans on people who block Yemeni ports or humanitarian relief deliveries, threaten aid workers, or undermine the UN peace process.

Amends the Global Magnitsky Act to require sanctions, within 30 days, on any foreign person — including Saudi officials or royal family members — responsible for or complicit in Jamal Khashoggi's death.

The arms ban can be waived only if the administration certifies the Saudi coalition has sustained a complete ceasefire and stopped obstructing cargo into Yemen for 180 days, with the government auditor checking the certification.
Sanctions supporters of the Houthis are also included, but the bill exempts acts needed to deliver urgently needed humanitarian assistance.

analysis.who_pays: US defense contractors that sell weapons to Saudi Arabia would lose sales until the ban expires in 2020; the Saudi government and royal family would face sanctions and lose US refueling support; Iran-linked networks aiding the Houthis would face new sanctions as well.
analysis.who_pays_short: Arms makers selling to Saudi Arabia

drawbacks.text: The arms suspension is temporary — it expires September 30, 2020 — and carves out ground-based missile defense sales, so it delays rather than permanently ends US weapons flows to Riyadh.
Cutting off US arms could push Saudi Arabia toward other suppliers or reduce US diplomatic influence with a key partner, a cost defenders of the relationship would argue cuts both ways.
New sanctions on people supporting the Houthis could chill business and aid activity in contested parts of Yemen, though the bill exempts humanitarian assistance from those sanctions.
The sanctions depend heavily on presidential enforcement determinations, which the administration of the day could interpret narrowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The human stakes — a famine-level humanitarian crisis fueled in part by US-supplied and US-fueled bombing — are far larger than the economic cost to a handful of arms exporters, especially since missile-defense sales are exempted and the ban sunsets in 2020. The bill is designed with real checks: the waiver requires an actual ceasefire verified by the government auditor. The honest caveat is that sanctions only bite if the President enforces them, and the same administration the bill was pressuring would be administering it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on November 15, 2018, the committee never took it up, and Congress ended January 3, 2019, so it died with no vote ever being scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 15, 2018 by Senator Menendez, joined on introduction by Senators Young, Reed, Graham, Shaheen, and Collins — a mix of three Republicans and three Democrats.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Foreign Relations.
No further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — appears in the action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The 115th Congress session dates confirm the bill sat for only the final weeks of the session, roughly seven weeks.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US defense contractors and the Saudi government came out ahead: American weapons sales to Riyadh and US military support for the coalition continued unimpeded, and no US sanctions were ever mandated for Khashoggi's killers or those blocking Yemen aid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arms contractors and the Saudi government

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, sponsoring the arms suspension, Yemen aid sanctions, and Khashoggi sanctions.

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan support from a leading defense hawk.

for.name: Sens. Todd Young (R-IN), Jack Reed (D-RI), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), and Susan Collins (R-ME)

against.name: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 15, 2018 and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed restricting arms sales to Saudi Arabia and sanctioning Saudi leadership over the Khashoggi killing, and defended continued US support for the Saudi-led coalition.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with three Republican cosponsors — including Lindsey Graham and Susan Collins — so support crossed party lines; with no vote ever held, there is no roll-call record of the split.

industries.note: The bill bars most weapons sales and export licenses to Saudi Arabia through September 2020, cutting into one of the largest US arms export relationships. Contractors' interest in keeping those sales running ran directly against stopping the bombing of Yemeni civilians with US-supplied weapons.

The bill mandates sanctions and visa bans on Saudi officials and royals responsible for Khashoggi's death, requires reports on Saudi human rights abuses, and ends US refueling of Saudi aircraft. Its interest in avoiding those consequences ran against accountability for the Yemen war.

industries.industry: Networks supplying the Houthis, including Iranian-linked actors
industries.note: The bill requires sanctions on anyone materially supporting the Houthis with weapons or funds, though it exempts urgently needed humanitarian work. Here the bill's pressure falls on actors obstructing or militarizing the conflict rather than on civilians.
